catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-john-xix:
Pope John XIX, enthroned in 1024, dead in 1032, shares one entry with John XX. A listed pope who never lived scrambled the Johns' numbering. When the last Crescentius patricius died, Tusculum's counts grabbed Rome's reins. One of their line climbed as Benedict VIII, while his brother Romanus wielded temporal power as consul and senator.

After Benedict died, Romanus, still a layman, won election between 12 April and 10 May 1024. He took every order in turn, assumed John's name, and courted Romans with lavish spending. Soon the Byzantine Emperor Basil II sent envoys begging the pope to acknowledge the oecumenical patriarch's title, bearing rich gifts to sway him. The talks stayed secret at first, but once the matter surfaced, public feeling forced John to turn down the Byzantine bids and gifts.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-john-xxi:
Pope John XXI, Lisbon-born between 1210 and 1220, took the throne in 1276 and died at Viterbo 20 May 1277. Julianus fathered him; baptised Peter, he went by Petrus Juliani or Petrus Hispanus. Lisbon's cathedral school gave him his first lessons, then Paris University, where he heard dialectics, logic, and above all Aristotelian physics and metaphysics from Albertus Magnus.

Natural philosophy drew Peter most. He took up medicine and theology, joining the Minorite master John of Parma. Once his studies ended, Siena's university, then fast growing, called him in 1247 to teach medicine. There he composed his Summulae logicales, logic's favourite textbook for almost three hundred years. The book tracks the Paris method and William Shyreswood's compendium, Shyreswood being Peter's teacher there. At Siena he also gathered a sheaf of medical prescriptions.
